speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In Singapore, it is difficult to imagine the circumstances under which the powers in this Bill would be required.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We see news reports of gunmen attacks, hostage incidents.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But they are happening elsewhere, not in Singapore.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: The closest we came was when we uncovered the Jemaah Islamiyah (JI) bombing plot.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Our security agencies picked it up, acted swiftly and, as a result, we avoided a calamity.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: That happened in 2001, well over a decade ago.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But for those who do remember, the thought may still send a chill down their spine.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Last year, another chilling piece of news emerged.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: She became radicalised and made plans to travel to Syria to support the Islamic State in Iraq and Syria (ISIS), to be a martyr’s widow.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In all these cases, our security agencies managed to intervene in time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But we may not be so fortunate every time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Because a terror attack has not happened in Singapore yet, it is difficult to appreciate the severity of the threat and to imagine the grave consequences.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: But Mr Speaker, the reality is that Singapore faces a clear and continuing threat.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Foreign terrorists see Singapore as a prized target.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We stand for many things in opposition to their ideology.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: We should, therefore, not be lulled into a false sense of security.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2016, the Police introduced new capabilities to allow them to respond swiftly to an attack, and they continue to enhance these capabilities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: In 2017, the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) amended the Public Order Act (POA) to enhance the security for large-crowd events.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: Did we not update POA just last year?

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They provide many useful lessons which are relevant to this debate, and I would like to share them with Members.

speaker: The Second Minister for Home Affairs (Mrs Josephine Teo)
text: They will help illustrate the gaps we have in our present laws.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Boston Police narrowed the suspects to a pair of brothers, Tamerlan and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the residential area of Watertown, the suspects got into a shootout with the police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Tamerlan was killed and 15 officers were injured.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Dzhokhar escaped and the police had to mount a house-to-house search.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During this time, the police issued a voluntary stay-in-place request within a 20-block area.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Despite this request by the police, some residents still ventured outdoors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Part of the reason could be because, as you can see in the photo on the right, there was no large-scale public disorder and the streets did not look dangerous.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The fact that the fugitive Dzhokhar was armed, had shot and killed one police officer, was not obvious.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Regular people who ventured outdoors, in spite of the police request, unknowingly affected police operations, which became much more difficult to manage.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They also put their own lives at great risk.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We would not, like the Boston Police, have been able to enforce a curfew in the search area to facilitate the manhunt operation and keep people safe from danger.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second example, January 2015, gunmen attacks in Paris.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On 7 January, two armed attackers entered the headquarters of the French satirical newspaper, Charlie Hebdo.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They killed 12, injured 11, and then fled.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Several shootouts took place, as the police pursued them across north-eastern France.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The two gunmen were killed two days later, after police stormed the building in which they were hiding.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On that same day, a third gunman walked into a Jewish supermarket, and took hostages.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In total, 17 were killed and 11 injured.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The French Police had to pursue the suspects over many areas quickly to prevent them from killing more.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The point is this: incidents can evolve very quickly; the theatre of operations also shifts quickly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Minister would have to make new proclamations to bring the powers to bear in every new incident area every time the operations shift to the new location.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police response would be much less timely.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another problem was the live news footages showing police officers ready to storm the supermarket to rescue hostages.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this photo, Members can see how the police were gathering outside the supermarket and they were getting ready to storm the place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But the terrorist was able to open fire at the police officers as soon as they started moving in.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He was waiting for the precise moment to strike, and he could.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In a situation like this, the terrorist had every possibility of watching every move of the police’s operation, as it happened.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This would compromise the tactical options that the police could take and risk the success of the operation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It also put the lives of the officers and hostages in greater danger.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The US Homeland Security Advisory Council studied this incident and published a White Paper in 2016.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One of the lessons the Council pointed out was the need to reduce the risk of information about police tactics being leaked and compromising operations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We would be wise to learn this lesson for Singapore, too.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In several overseas incidents, police forces had appealed to the public not to transmit or broadcast videos of ongoing operations, to protect the safety of their officers and the public.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Cases of individuals and media knowingly transmitting and broadcasting are common, even when they are told that the information may lead to the loss of lives.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They happened in developed and cosmopolitan cities like Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: New threats call for new measures to better protect Singaporeans and save lives when we come under attack.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Having explained today's threat and why we need POSSPA, let me outline the situations where POSSPA can be activated, what tools Police will be given in this Bill to respond effectively to a serious incident, how these tools will be activated, and safeguards against abuse.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: POPA was enacted in 1958, and there have been no major reviews of POPA since.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It was designed to deal with large-scale communal riots, such as the serious racial clashes in Penang, during the Centenary Celebrations in Georgetown in January 1957, the year before.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under POPA, Police have special powers to deal with serious threats to public order, for example, to impose curfews and disperse assemblies.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As there is already a legal framework within POPA that contains the necessary special powers in one Act, MHA is updating this framework to ensure that we remain effective to tackle the evolving security threats.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I explained through the examples, the security threats and challenges have evolved.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In addition to large-scale public disorder, we also have to deal with violent extremism.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is necessary because there may not always be public order problems in, say, a manhunt following a terror attack, such as in the Boston Marathon bombings.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The term "serious incident" is clearly defined in clause 3.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What are the additional powers provided under POSSPA that will enable the Police to protect public order and safety, in the event of a serious incident?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will, first, talk about the new tools introduced in POSSPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The first set of tools deals with modern technologies which can endanger the safety of the public and security forces.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Sixty years ago, when POPA was enacted, there were only landline telephones.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, we have smartphones, the Internet, 24/7 television news channels, and drones.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Everyone with a smartphone can broadcast, and very many do, sometimes with wider viewership than regular media channels.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such modern technologies have been both a boon and a bane for the Police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One clear example when they can hinder Police operations is during sensitive tactical operations, like hostage rescue.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police need to have the element of surprise over the perpetrators, so that the latter will not start to harm the victims in anticipation of the Police's response or prepare themselves to defeat Police action.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The best-laid plans for the Police can be thwarted by a stray tweet or social media livestream, but the existing laws, such as the POA may not allow the Police to deal adequately with such risks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During a serious incident, the Police will need every help they can get to be able to successfully execute their mission to save lives.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: POSSPA, therefore, contains special powers, to reduce the risk that their operations are compromised by unauthorised communications.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Of these powers, the power to make a Communications Stop Order has garnered the most attention following the introduction of the Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would, therefore, like to spend some time to explain this power carefully.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The CSO is not an information blackout throughout a terror incident, as some have portrayed it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The CSO will only apply to coverage of the target area.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After the security operations are over, the CSO will be lifted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even with a CSO, post-incident reporting is still necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, the Police will allow selected media access to incident locations, so that the events can still be recorded for subsequent use.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We had conveyed this arrangement to senior editors and reporters of our local media at various engagements last month.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also informed some of the foreign media here of our plans and how we will do our best to facilitate coverage.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I should add that the CSO is a discretionary power which can only be exercised by the Commissioner of Police under specific conditions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clause 30 allows the Commissioner to make such an order only if he assesses that the communication of information about the target area or law enforcement operations compromises the operations or endangers the safety of people during the operations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police will publicise the CSO and state clearly the time that it becomes effective, and the boundaries of the target area.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Having said that, let me give this assurance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The CSO is not aimed at civilians who, for example, may be caught in a hostage situation, and are trying to get information about their predicament to security forces by any means possible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead, we are trying to stop irresponsible communication of ongoing security operations which may endanger lives, such as those of the hostages.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some have asked, "What if someone was merely filming and not transmitting?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That, surely, should not be a problem." The problem, I am afraid, is that in a situation that warrants a CSO, the Police will not have the luxury of time to confirm that everyone was merely filming to document the event and that no one was attempting to share valuable intelligence with the terrorists.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The more important question is this: when lives are at stake, should we hope for the best or must we assume the worst, that someone, somewhere, had malicious intent?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even if the Police were to order anyone they can see holding a camera to stop filming, as they can under the POA, what about people with small devices which Police did not notice amid the chaos?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Should the onus be on the Police to identify everyone who is filming and stop them, or should the onus be on individuals not to arouse suspicion of their intent?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We hope we will never have to issue a CSO.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If ever there was a need, half measures will not cut it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even with a CSO, we can only reduce but not fully eradicate the risk of unauthorised communications.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is something we need to bear in mind.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: UAVs and AVs can be used for surveillance, and even as weapons.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under today's laws, the Police can take down UAVs and AVs only if they are clearly posing a threat to public safety and security.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is also aimed at preventing the compromise of operations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We recognise the significant impact on the public if and when clause 32 is invoked.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is, therefore, a higher threshold in place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Direction can only be issued by the Minister.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is unlike other special powers that, once unlocked by the Activation Order, can be authorised by the Commissioner of Police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where the Communications Stop Order is sufficient and effective, there will be no need for a Direction to withdraw telecommunications services.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Their main concerns were how to operationalise the Direction, and how to communicate the disruption to clients.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police will work closely with the Infocomm Media Development Authority (IMDA) and the telcos to develop plans and conduct exercises to ensure that a Direction can be implemented effectively.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The second tool, in clauses 16 and 17 of the Bill, provides enhanced powers to stop and question individuals in a target area.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police may need, for example, to ascertain the purpose for their presence in the area or to get information which might help the Police in their operations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under POSSPA, refusal to provide the required information will be an offence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is to empower the Police to get as much relevant information as possible in a timely way.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The third tool helps the Police to manage buildings in the area affected by the serious incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where it is necessary to close the premises or restrict entry, the Police will generally work closely with premises owners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is not a problem if premises owners are cooperative.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If, however, premises owners are uncooperative, clause 27 provides powers to the Police to direct premises owners to close the premises, restrict entry or provide information and documents relating to the premises.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As military premises are sensitive locations, the Police will work closely with the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) to manage any serious incidents affecting these premises, so that there will not be a need to use the clause 27 power in such circumstances.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During a serious incident, we may need to tap on additional resources to assist the Police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are established plans for SAF to assist the Home Team in responding to serious security incidents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under POPA, SAF servicemen were authorised with powers of search, arrest and to set up cordons.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clause 15 similarly empowers other law enforcement officers and civilian assistants to support the Police operations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Law enforcement officers refer to officers from other Home Team agencies, such as the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority (ICA), the Central Narcotics Bureau (CNB) and the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police may also ask civilian assistants, such as the Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) volunteers and private security officers, to help, for example, to man an outer cordon, away from the incident location or hot zone, or prevent persons from entering the cordoned area.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This allows Police resources to be diverted to more critical tasks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I should highlight that nothing in POSSPA obliges civilians to assist the Police, and neither will the Police request for civilian assistance where there may be danger.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police will only rely on civilians who are able and willing to assist.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In other words, a civilian can refuse to assist, and no action will be taken against him.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As spelt out in subsection (4) of clause 15, civilian assistants can only exercise a limited set of powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They are not allowed, for example, to use lethal force.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under clause 51, law enforcement officers, SAF servicemen and civilians who are assisting Police Officers are granted protection from legal liability.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is so long as they act in good faith and with reasonable care.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This legal protection extends to members of the public who are complying with the Police's orders or directions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: POSSPA also retains and updates the existing provisions from POPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These provide tools which are still relevant for Police operations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will talk about some of the key provisions that have been updated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, the powers to impose cordons under clause 18.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was provided for under POPA, section 6.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It has been updated to allow the Police to set up a cordon within a private place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was provided for under POPA, section 11.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: During a serious incident, the Police may require the use of equipment, electricity or space within a premises or land in the target area.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have retained the compensation framework in POPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Thirdly, the use of lethal weapons as a last resort.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In every circumstance today, lethal weapons can only be used after all other available options have been exhausted, or when it is absolutely necessary, such as for time-critical situations, where the safety and security of the public are at risk.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When a serious incident has occurred, or is about to occur, the Police will use all available force options to deal with the incident, including lethal weapons as a last resort.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are two parts to the updated powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Part 1, the use of lethal weapons in certain circumstances, which was provided for under POPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under POPA, the Police can use up to lethal force, as reasonably necessary, to prevent persons from entering the cordoned area.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Part 2, on the use of lethal weapons to effect arrest and prevent escape from the arrest.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The use of lethal weapons is not taken lightly, and the Police have been careful at all times to first exhaust other means.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This high standard of care will be maintained even in a serious incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is to reflect the seriousness of the offences and is in line with similar provisions, such as the Infrastructure Protection Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: POSSPA pools together the necessary tools and places these in one coherent piece of legislation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: How will the Police gain access to these tools?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: When an incident has happened or is being threatened, the Police will deal with it using their baseline policing powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, if the incident is serious, and the Police assess that they need the special powers under POSSPA, they will recommend to the Minister to activate POSSPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After considering the Police's assessment, the Minister can issue an Activation Order under clause 8, if he is of the opinion that: (a) There is a serious incident occurring, or one has occurred, or there is a threat of a serious incident occurring, in Singapore; and (b) The exercise of any power in POSSPA is necessary to substantially assist in preventing the incident or reducing the impact of the incident, or to control, restore and maintain public order.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Both conditions have to be met before the Minister can issue an Activation Order.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Activation Order unlocks a range of special powers, which I have explained earlier, which the Police will need to deal with during the serious incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But it is important to note that these special powers will not automatically come into force upon the issuance of the Activation Order by the Minister.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Each special power has to be specifically unlocked by the Commissioner of Police only as and when deemed necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under clause 11, the Commissioner of Police issues a Special Authorisation that can target a specific area, person, and/or vehicle.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Commissioner may declare more than one target area, target person or target vehicle, depending on the operational need.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Minister for Home Affairs will publicise the Activation Order in accordance with clause 8 subsection (2), for example, through the media via press releases, and online and social media platforms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We do not intend to use the POSSPA powers for longer than is absolutely necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After a serious incident has been resolved, we would want to work with the affected communities to return to normalcy as soon as possible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By necessity, the provisions of the Bill are crafted broadly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is because the threat situation continues to evolve and, quite frankly, the methods deployed by terrorists are increasingly hard to predict.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Through POSSPA, we will provide the Police the tools they need to respond effectively to a serious incident, and some degree of latitude in exercising the special powers when they are activated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: First, as I described earlier, there is a two-tier unlocking mechanism in POSSPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Not all of the special powers will be used in every case.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Even after the Minister has issued the Activation Order on the request of the Police, the Commissioner must apply his mind, and decide: (a) which of the special powers are needed to respond to the serious incident, (b) who may exercise these powers, and (c) which area, person or vehicle these powers may apply to.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Second, the law also sets out clear criteria which must be met by the Minister and the Commissioner of Police before they issue the Activation Order or Special Authorisation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Third, even on the ground, the law sets out clear criteria and limits for Police officers to adhere to, in their exercise of these powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, the basis for removing a vehicle, and how they may remove a vehicle from a target area, are set out quite clearly in clause 24 (1) and (2).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Police officers are also subject to internal guidelines and rules of engagement in their exercise of powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Parliament has not been and is not prevented from holding Ministers to account for decisions or policies, just because there are no specific provisions in the law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But let me return to why we have the Bill in the first place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the Paris attacks of November 2015, the first incident occurred outside a football stadium.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Within minutes, there was shooting on the streets.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Long before anyone could make sense of what was going on, hostages had been taken at a theatre.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To save lives, the Police will have to act fast.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Should we build in additional layers of approval, for example, to require Parliament to confirm the Minister’s activation or the Commissioner's authorisations even while the situation is unfolding?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In Singapore's case, I believe the latter is better able to serve our interests and I hope Members can support this view.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore is an international hub and a multiracial and multi-religious society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have a good reputation; the society is stable, and people generally feel safe.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Because of these attributes, we are a prized target for terrorists.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Being able to successfully attack Singapore will give terrorists significant advantage in advancing their cause and reputation, and it will be a major victory for the terrorists.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Terror attacks follow the same game play of division, terror, pandemonium.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But terror attacks have ranged in form, such as lone wolf attacks, for example, knife attacks against a church in Yogyakarta, Indonesia; to coordinated firearm attacks, for example, the bombing in Paris in November 2015; or the tactic of long besiegement, for example, in Marawi, Philippines, or a quick single attack through commonplace items, for example, the vehicle rampage in Berlin's Christmas market; or highly symbolic, high impact attacks, for example, the collapse of the Twin Towers, or insidious attacks against innocent children, such as the bombing at the Ariana Grande concert.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As terrorists' methods change and vary widely, we, too, in Singapore, need to ensure that our laws keep abreast to deal with their widening and changing modus operandi.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These have been carefully defined under clauses 3 and 4.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While such expanded powers are completely ill-suited for a neighbourhood theft incident, for example, the standard powers are also ill-suited for dealing with such large-scale public order and public safety events.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For example, under clause 19, read with clause 15(4)(a), the Police are able to rope in civilians to help to cordon off roads.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would be extremely useful, for example, where there is a large area to secure and when back-up is not there yet, and time is of the essence in preventing the perpetrator from escaping or other members of the public from entering.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another example is the power to remove parked vehicles under clause 24 on the basis of endangering others, obstructing traffic flow and hindering the exercise of special powers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Imagine what would happen if a single vehicle held up the back-up Police forces, or if a vehicle was lying around as a getaway car, also doubling up as an obstruction to Police forces.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another example is the power under clause 27 to direct premises owners to cooperate by providing information about the premises, closing the premises for a specific time, and ensuring the entrances and exits are secured.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Take, for example, a situation where the perpetrator is still at large in the area.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Surely, we do not want more people walking into the "minefield".

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, although it is predicated on the Minister's issuance of an "activation order", which powers are to be exercised and by whom, are decisions for the Police Commissioner to make.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is done, not by the Minister, but by the Police Commissioner separately issuing temporary restraining orders, communication stop orders and requisition powers as well as the "special authorisation" under clause 11.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Importantly, the current Bill is not without safeguards, as alluded to by the good Minister.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is not a rough expansion of powers across the board, carte blanche.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, while the Police are able to enforce curfew orders, serviceman cannot.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Furthermore, other countermeasures in the Bill, such as curfews, communication stop orders, discontinuation of telecommunication service, requisition powers, do not apply across the board.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They require yet another order by the Commissioner or Minister, on top of the more general conferring of broader powers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This calibrated approach makes sure that the measures are flexible enough to be effective in different situations, in different scenarios.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: An activation order or a mere special authorisation is not a free pass to all the rest of the countermeasure powers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They require additional orders by the Minister or Commissioner, only arising when the situation calls for it and may apply for a shorter time period.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are not treating it as a one-size-fits-all authorisation, but we are ensuring that there are enough mechanisms to address serious incidents effectively.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another important restriction that embeds accountability into the exercise of power is the explicit lists of acceptable purposes of the use of the power.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Take, for example, the communications stop order in clause 30.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In a "serious incident" like that in illustration (d) of a large sit-down demonstration impeding traffic and interfering with normal business activities, it seems a communication stop order is not to be issued to quell publicity.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather, it appears that it can only be issued if it is in the Police Commissioner's opinion that it would endanger safety of the public, prejudices ongoing law enforcement activity and other purposes set out in clause 30(2)(b).

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Perpetrators at the Taj and Oberoi hotels in Mumbai in 2008 were able to view and monitor actions of security forces through television (TV) coverage.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Once a theatre of threat has been established, we should remove all disadvantages to the Police.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: That will help to quell the threat and neutralise the danger.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This restriction on communication protects the people being rescued by increasing the chances of a successful rescue.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also protects the people who are trying to rescue them.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: After all, they, too, have families and friends waiting for their safe return.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as important as it is to control the physical situation, it is also important for the right foundations to be laid for social resilience.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: If there is a vacuum of information, there may be a lack of confidence that the situation is being managed.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another countermeasure that may be utilised is the power of requisition under clause 35.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One can imagine that in a densely built-up urban area, such as Singapore, this power may be especially important for launching an effective surprise attack on the target person.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Bill also provides for additional offences that seek to ensure that the situation in the target area does not escalate further.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For instance, clause 37, relating to provoking breach of peace.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While "reasonable steps" have been defined under clause 46(6) through the "standard provision" relating to corporate crimes as stated in the Explanatory Statement, what would it look like for a company to do all reasonable steps to promote a culture, something that is built over time, that does not encourage, tolerate or lead to noncompliance of the offences when the offences under this Bill only arise under the special circumstances of an activation order?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope the Minister will be able to clarify.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: From a macro perspective, Mr Speaker, this Bill confers powers necessary to effectively deal with large-scale public order, public safety threats.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It comes with an underlying tension, and I accept that.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: On the one hand, we do not want to face a situation where the Police is unable to neutralise the danger and quell the disorder because they lack the necessary powers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And, on the other hand, there may be sentiments that the Police should not be given disproportionate powers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In my view, this Bill equips the Police with a level of power necessary to quell danger and neutralise an escalating threat.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The foundation of my argument is that we have a good Police Force which largely enforce their powers professionally.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Two weeks later, on 15 March, MHA repeated that the Bill would not apply to day-to-day policing.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This second statement was made in response to concerns from civil society groups about the wide wording of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, the Second Minister has just repeated the assurance in her Second Reading speech when she said she hoped that the Special Powers would never need to be used.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As MHA has stated, the threshold for special powers to be activated in the Bill is "high".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The powers under this Bill must never be misused for situations that can be adequately dealt with under other laws.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This Bill serves to repeal the POPA enacted in 1958, but its aims are wider.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the long title of POPA states that the Act relates to the maintenance and restoration of public order, this Bill states that its aim is to "extend Police powers to better prevent and respond to any incident or likely incident involving serious violence or large-scale public disorder in Singapore".

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thus, this Bill envisages prevention and response, not just to public disorder, but serious violence as well.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, the Bill provides some new powers not contained in POPA, such as the ability of the Police to direct owners of buildings within incident areas to take actions like closing the building for a specified time, and for the Police to question individuals within a target area when conducting a manhunt.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government would need muscle as well as flexibility to respond quickly and effectively to those threats.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to clause 9, the Minister's Activation Order must specify the nature of the serious incident, the duration of the Activation Order, and authorise the Commissioner of Police to exercise all or any of the Special Powers under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It seems to me that the principle of proportionality should be a cardinal principle in exercising all the powers under the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Not only must the Minister’s threshold for issuing an Activation Order be high, the decision of which Special Powers are really needed to deal with a particular scenario should be deliberately considered case by case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Earlier during the Second Minister's Second Reading speech, she confirmed that, for each incident, the Commissioner of Police would consider the need for each Special Power as commensurate with the nature of the incident.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What should also concern us today is whether any of the provisions in the Bill seem to be too wide or involve too much of a compromise on competing public interests, such as public accountability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In this regard, I have two concerns to raise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the definition of "serious incident" under clause 3 of the Bill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There are five factual illustrations for the scope of clause 3.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first three scenarios concern the use of explosives and firearms, and the forcible taking over of public transport, which, to most of us, warrant an exceptional response from the authorities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the last two illustrations which concern public disorder are more controversial.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Illustration (e) is about a group protesting in the street that grows in size and then starts to commit violent acts, which sounds to me like rioting, which is an arrestable offence under the Penal Code.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I would like the Minister to explain why the existing laws are not adequate to deal with such scenarios as in illustrations (d) and (e).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Commissioner can issue a CSO if he is of the view that exhibiting or communicating such relevant pictures, films, texts or audio messages would prejudice ongoing law enforcement operations relating to serious incidents or endanger the safety of the public or law enforcement officers during the law enforcement activity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The terms "relevant picture or film", and "relevant text or audio message", are defined in clause 2 broadly to mean those made while the Special Powers are activated and which are related to the target area or law enforcement activities in the target area.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under clause 31, a Police Officer can direct persons to stop making, exhibiting or communicating such relevant films, pictures, texts or audio messages.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Police can also compel the deletion and the surrender of such material, and require persons to provide information on the recipients of any communications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, in 2009, a Group of Twenty (G20) summit meeting was held in London and a police operation codenamed "Operation Glencoe" was mounted to manage protestors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the operation was on, a man named Ian Tomlinson suddenly fell and died while in the vicinity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Police initially denied that they had any altercation with him, until a video taken by an American there on business, showed Mr Tomlinson being pushed to the ground by police.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This led to inquiries that uncovered the truth, which would not have happened had contemporaneous videos not been recorded.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the reality is that in any investigation, evidence talks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If it is a case of "he-says-she-says", the burden will fall on the complainant to prove the complaint.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I note what the Second Minister had said earlier in her Second Reading speech about the operational difficulties that the Police may face on the ground to distinguish between who is simply just making a film for record, or who is contemporaneously transmitting the films.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As a former Police Officer, I understand that difficulty fully.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: While I recognise that in emergency situations, there is a need for the authorities to act swiftly and given some latitude in exercising their powers, we must nonetheless ensure that such security measures remain accountable and be accorded with due process and fairness so as to ensure that public confidence in the Government does not erode during crisis time.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Before I turn to discuss the substance of the Bill, I would like to understand if there was a public consultation for this Bill.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I believe the public has a right to have their views heard on this Bill before its enactment, given that this Bill is a matter of public interest because it has wide-ranging implications and would intimately affect the public during emergency situations.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: One of the concerns that I have was the definition of what constitutes a "serious incident".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: So, what in this illustration would make it a "serious" enough incident such that it could be comparable to the other illustrations, such as illustrations (a) and (b), both depicting possible terrorist attacks?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Illustration (d) is a peaceful protest involving neither violence against any person or property damage and presumably attracting a substantial level of support.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: While such events may require some Police intervention because of some degree of disorderliness, but they are not comparable to armed attacks or hostage situations in terms of severity.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: To me, illustration (d) seems to stand in stark contrast to all the other illustrations provided, as the level of severity and the threat posed is significantly lower.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Another area of concern that I have with the Bill is that it enlists the help of civilian assistants to discharge certain duties.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Under clause 2 of the Bill, specific powers are given to civilian assistants to assist a Police Officer who is granted the special authorisation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Further, under clause 15(4)(a), a civilian assistant is authorised to exercise certain powers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, in emergency situations that require instant decision-making under pressure, there is a possibility that civilian assistants might not possess the ability to respond quickly, decisively and even correctly as a trained personnel would.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, civilian assistants may exacerbate the emergency situation or inadvertently cause harm to themselves or bystanders while discharging their duties.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: As such, my concern is that enlisting of the assistance of civilian assistants might be more detrimental than beneficial during a crisis period and that the safety of these assistants might be compromised in the process of discharging their duties.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I would, therefore, like to understand how the Ministry will ensure that the safety of these assistants is protected when they discharge their duties.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Under clause 8 of the Bill, if, in the opinion of the Minister, the granting of the Activation Order is necessary to prevent or reduce the impact of the serious incident or to control or maintain public order after the serious incident, my question is, what does the term "necessary" entail?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Comparatively, under the Criminal Law (Temporary Provisions) Act and the Internal Security Act (ISA), both of which are security-nature Acts, the decisions of the Minister are subject to the concurrence by the President on the advice of a special advisory committee.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Just now, in the Second Minister's Second Reading speech, she has articulated the reason why she felt this should be removed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: While I understand the time sensitivity of the Special Order, however, I also note the Second Minister has also said, this is such a special situation that she would even wish that it would not be ever activated.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I think a mechanism of accountability should have been there.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It can be done as soon as possible, without impeding the expediency of the Police when they are exercising this Order.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: If it is a must to publish an Activation Order, logic dictates that the failure to publish the Order will invalidate it.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Such a failure to publish means that the public may be uninformed.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How can someone be held liable for a sudden change they have not been reasonably notified about?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, if there is a situation when there is a failure to publish such a notice, should there not be a system of accountability of why the failure happened?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Now, I would like to discuss the next area of concern which pertains to clauses 30 and 31 which give the Commissioner the power to make CSOs against individuals.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the MHA's Press Release on 27 February 2018, the Ministry explained that such a CSO is necessary to prevent leakage of such information to terrorist which could endanger the lives of security officers and members of the public who are caught in the act.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: The Ministry cited two examples: that of the Mumbai and Paris attacks whereby live television and media broadcast during those attacks resulted in leakage of information to the terrorists.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In turn, such leakage of information made the police operation more difficult and placed the safety of the officers and hostages at greater risk.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In both incidents, it was not individual communications between persons or through the social media that impeded security operations, but rather through the live reporting of the said incidents by the media.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: There might also be issues arising from the issuance of CSOs against individuals.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: How is that individual then going to report to the Ministry when the only evidence to substantiate that claim has been deleted?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister please clarify what will be done in such a situation?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the event of "serious incidents", like terrorist attacks, there will be a lot of confusion, and emotion will run high.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, the impact of any such security incidents is not just about fatalities and loss of properties, but it will cause fear and distress and then destabilise, paralyse and even divide the society.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the aftermath of such an event, it is important that there is enough information for us to piece things together, to verify facts, to dismiss accusations and restore justice if need be.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Hence, in these moments of high tension when people think that it is important to document certain happenings so that it could be useful in the aftermath of the event, to help the Police to understand the situations better, this CSO should not deter the individuals from doing that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, documentation is important in the event of allegations of whether the Police or the public have stepped out of their line.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is a means to protect Police Officers and the public from false accusations and these documentations are witnesses and testimonies and, in the aftermath of the event, can help a lot in the healing of the community.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: I have one more query pertaining to this.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: What if a Police Officer was accused of abuse of process by an individual who has documented the incident during the effect of the CSO could prove that the Police was innocent, would this individual who surrenders the documentation then be charged?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Another operational issue that I have is with the power of the Minister to give directions to telecommunication licensees to, amongst others, stop messages carried by a telecommunication service provided by the licensee under clause 32(3)(a) or prohibit the use of telecommunications by the licensee when an activation order is in effect.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: In the event that the telecommunication messaging and telecommunications services are discontinued, how would individuals caught in the vicinity where the serious incident occurred be able to send out messages of distress or call for help?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: My final area of concern pertains to clause 38 of the Bill which criminalises, amongst others, the publication of materials prejudicial to public order.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: For instance, clause 38(1) (a) merely requires the said material to be "likely to be prejudicial", as opposed to being "highly likely to be prejudicial".

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: It is a trite criminal law principle that an individual must have a guilty mind in addition to his or her action before one can be criminalised.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, can the Minister provide reasons as to why clause 38(2) appears to deviate from this important principle?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Fourthly, Mr Speaker, I also note that in the interest of speed and efficiency, criminalising an individual under clause 38 may not necessarily be the most efficient measure to deal with materials that may be prejudicial to public order during an emergency situation.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Would a takedown order that immediately forces an individual to stop distributing or take down any prejudicial matter be faster and more efficient in dealing with the publication of such material rather than criminalising the conduct?

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: National security is a priority in the current global climate.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: However, my view is that the Bill affords too much discretion on decision-makers.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, more can be done in this respect to ensure greater transparency and accountability which are crucial during times of emergencies.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a former Police Officer myself, I can understand and appreciate fully the challenges faced by our Police Officers on the ground daily.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our Police Officers place their lives at risk constantly, and this risk increases immensely in the event of an attack.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While others are running away from the threat, our officers must run towards, and seek to diffuse the threat.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In my view, the powers proposed in this Bill are necessary and timely.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It will help our Police and other Home Team officers better carry out their job to save lives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore continues to be a prized target of regional and global terrorist organisations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over the years, our intelligence and law enforcement agencies have managed to act swiftly and discreetly to foil the attempts of foreign JI and ISIS militants in carrying out an attack in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But terrorism threats to our country are not confined to within our borders.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent years, we have also seen a rise in the number of self-radicalised individuals influenced by extremist ideologies to target Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Clearly, the threat to Singapore has increased tremendously, and our legislation needs to evolve in tandem to combat these threats.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I agree that this is important and time-critical for the Police, especially in the event of multiple attacks, such as the November 2015 attacks in Paris, which saw a series of coordinated terrorist attacks in multiple locations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, who makes the operational call that these multiple incidents are connected?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the May 2017 Manchester concert bombing, there was a separate security incident which prompted an evacuation of a shopping mall in Manchester.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Some thought that it was a coordinated attack, but investigations later revealed that it was unrelated to the concert bombing.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: My question then is whether the subsequent incidents must have a nexus to the original incident, or should the Minister be required to issue a new Activation Order if the subsequent incidents are seemingly unrelated to the first incident?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Who then makes the call if incidents are related or not to the first incident?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the manhunt for the Boston marathon bombers, "live" reports showing key police operations helped the suspects to evade capture for about four days.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the Manila bus hostage incident, the "live" broadcast of impending police operations to storm the bus further agitated the hostage-taker, who executed several hostages before he was eventually taken down.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Having a CSO imposed in such scenarios would help protect operation secrecy, prevent critical information from leaking to the suspects via the media and, more crucially, prevent the loss of innocent lives.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, it is a well-known fact that the initial 30 minutes after an incident occurs is a key period where every information collected is vital for the authorities to make sense of what is happening.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is also why our Police have been advocating the concept of Run, Hide and Tell.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Where possible, tell the Police as soon as you can on where you are and what is happening.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How can we, in the event of a terrorist incident, strike a balance between Run, Hide and Tell, with the imposition of a CSO?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Going back to the Boston Marathon bombing, the big breakthrough in identifying the suspects came from a photo taken by a spectator watching the race from across the street.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We would need to make sure that any communications ban would not inadvertently end up harming Police investigations.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, to do so, the Police Officer is required to locate the person operating the drone or autonomous vehicle.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Upcoming models will soon be able to operate beyond an operator's visual line of sight.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How would our Police Officers be able to find the drone operator if the drone in question is far away from the operator?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Similarly, autonomous vehicle technology is advancing towards a level of autonomy where a human will not be required to be in the car.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How would the Police Officer direct an autonomous vehicle away in such an instance?

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: These are questions that MHA would need to think about carefully, as technology advances.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The powers to protect the integrity of tactical operations will enable the Police to carry out their mission by choosing the best tactical options available, without having to worry that the terrorists can watch their actions "live", anticipate their actions, and ambush them around the next corner.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The proposed amendments serve to ensure that our Police will not be caught without the powers they require to safeguard lives and property, when an attack occurs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Keeping us safe and secure every day is not an easy task and our Home Team has done and continues to do an incredible job.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In view of the rising terrorism threats around the world, it is increasingly important to strengthen and tighten home security to ensure public order and safety.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: This is even more crucial for a small and multi-ethnic nation like Singapore.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Security is, indeed, a joint responsibility among individuals, community and the Government.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I, therefore, welcome the SGSecure national movement as Singapore's community response to the threat of terror.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In our workplaces, we have people of different races and nationalities working side by side.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The news on ISIS and self-radicalised individuals may affect the cohesion of the various groups of people working and living amongst us.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: It is, therefore, important that our officers are trained adequately to face potential challenges and different situations.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill is also essential to protect the secrecy of tactical operations and enable the Police to respond to serious incidents more effectively.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Does this include non-violent passive protest or demonstration that has serious societal implication besides violent or terrorist incidents?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Second, when the Commissioner of Police authorises a CSO while security operations are ongoing, it will require all people in the vicinity from not taking pictures of the incident or sending them across to others.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In today’s context, almost all Singaporeans use a mobile phone to inform their loved ones of their safety.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can such harmless communication be allowed if an individual is within the vicinity of the serious incident?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: More often than not, public information via social media may provide useful leads for Police investigations.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: With this Bill, the public may be wary of producing such information to the Police even if they had acquired them.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While we want to prevent frivolous dissemination of vital information, there should be means to acquire such useful information from the public.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should encourage civil society’s active participation in deterring terrorism and serious incidents with useful public information.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will the Bill discourage such responsive nature of public involvement to apprehend perpetrators?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Will such special powers result in public fear of abuse of power by the Police?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can one independently verify Police action when there is a communication blackout as the evidence presented is one-sided?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: The public must know the serious implications as it is now deemed an offence if one violates the order.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: While the public gets used to the new restriction, I hope that cases of genuine violation due to ignorance will be dealt minimally with discretionary powers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have to look to incidents around the world to learn about the evolving methods that terrorists use to inflict maximum damage and terror.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Even if these incidents have not occurred in Singapore, there is no guarantee that it will not happen here.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And when they do, we need to be prepared for it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The POSSPA Bill is an important step to equip and empower our security agencies to mount an effective response, should we one day need it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While I support the Bill in its intentions, allow me to seek a few clarifications on its details.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In clause 3, "serious incidents" are defined to constitute terrorist acts, acts of serious violence, acts causing large-scale public disorder, and so on.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Members of this House, past and present, have continuously debated about striking the right balance between maintaining public order and proportionate responses to achieving that order.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have constantly been recalibrating this balance, not just today, but in 2009 when we discussed the POA, and again in 2014 after the Little India Riots.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill provides an example of such an act, describing "a sit-down demonstration...(which) attracts a large group of sympathisers who voluntarily join the sit-in… Their presence starts to impede the flow of vehicular and pedestrian traffic", which many other Members of this House have quoted as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I would also like to seek clarity on the size of an assembly that could qualify as a "large-scale public disorder".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When would a crowd be large enough for these special powers to be activated?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Again, members of the public are clearly supportive of the use of lethal weapons to ensure compliance with orders when there is a terrorist attack but the concern of some members of the public is whether we need to use such lethal powers for a sit-down demonstration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I believe that the CSO in clause 30 is absolutely necessary in situations where "live" communications could give terrorists the upper hand.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We do not want to see an embarrassing repeat of the Mumbai attacks in 2008 or the Manila hostage crisis in 2010.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Related to my previous point, I would like to ask the rationale again for requiring such a stop order, again, for "acts causing large-scale public disorder".

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister provide some clarifications on why this is needed?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that a member of the public would not be penalised if he/she was taking a photo and sending it to the authorities via SGSecure.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In any given situation, there could be many people using their phones concurrently for different reasons, some violating the CSO and some not.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Furthermore, I believe it would be beneficial to have more clarity on certain language used in the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can it be more clearly defined as to what constitutes "reasonable force"?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While empowering the Police with necessary powers to maintain public order, we also need to balance this with safeguards to prevent the misuse of this power.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill now also grants some special powers to "civilian assistants", which Members of this House have raised as well, which I understand was not previously included in POPA.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How can we ensure that these civilian assistants are sufficiently trained, particularly to know what "reasonable force" entails?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some members of the public are also concerned that with the CSO, if any cases of potential Police brutality were to occur, we would not have independent documentation of the event.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This may lead to some questions on whether there are sufficient safeguards to prevent a scenario of disproportionate power.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we will have to bear in mind that they may not be in possession of any evidence to support that Police report, due to the CSO.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many other countries have similarly stepped up their counter-terrorism responses, such as the EU countries which have been victims of horrific attacks.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Britain, for instance, under its Investigative Powers Act, is empowered to conduct mass surveillance.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While we agree that the Police need to have sweeping powers under the extraordinary circumstance of a terrorist attack, we also need to have safeguards to provide a sense of balance.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I will approach the Bill on two aspects.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: First, on the special authorisation and, next, on the CSO.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On the special authorisation by the Commissioner of Police under the Bill, I would like to clarify the following issues with the Minister. “A law enforcement officer is defined in clause 2(1) to mean a Police Officer, an immigration officer, a narcotics officer, a prisons officer or a Civil Defence Service officer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The class may be expanded by the Minister”, as cited in the explanatory notes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How does the Minister envisage the class to be expanded?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The second group of people who can exercise the special powers specified in the special authorisation under subsection 1(c) refers to servicemen or SAF personnel and they "do not act on the direction and in aid of the Police Officer given the authorisation".

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How would the Police and SAF coordinate the operations on the ground?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Would it be coordinated by Ministers or by a Ministerial Committee or by the Cabinet?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The third group who can exercise the special powers is made of any civilian, cited as a civilian assistant.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I note that Minister has clarified that they can include security guards.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: How are the security guards organised during peace time so that they can better assist the Police during a crisis?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Lastly, under the scope of the Bill, apart from obvious terrorist attacks where injuries and outright threats to public safety are apparent, it also listed an example of a sit-down demonstration where vehicles or pedestrians may be obstructed but public safety may not be threatened.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Why would such incidents fall under this Bill, which has been enacted specifically for counter-terrorism purposes?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Moreover, the Police already have the power to deal with a sit-down demonstration under the ambit of unlawful assembly, for example, as defined in the Penal Code.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The CSO's main objective is to deprive terrorists or criminals of information.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It will also deny the terrorists the opportunity to broadcast their terrorist acts "live" through the media, like the case of the Mumbai attacks in 2008.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But the CSO is a very blunt instrument.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In order to assure the public that the CSO would not be abused and that there are safeguards in place, I hope the Minister could address and respond to the following two points.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Hence, it appears harsh to ban the media professionals from doing their jobs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We note that the Police are the only party that would be allowed to make any recordings of the scene when the special powers are exercised.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I hope the Minister can direct the Police to release the full footage after the event so that it would not lead to a gap in the documentation of Singapore’s history for future generations and this would also help to counter criticism of any abuse by the Police during the Police operations.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While not a legal instrument of force, its recommendations for journalists bear thinking about as a possible guide for journalists to be allowed to do their jobs responsibly during such incidents.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These include responsible coverage of the event lest the perpetrators are watching and careful phrasing of events so as not to influence the public's perception.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: While I understand that not all media will cooperate and adhere to the code of conduct, but we should not give up trying and should only use the CSO as a last resort.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, the special powers, including the CSO given to the Police under this Bill are wide-ranging.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Could the Minister give us an idea whether there were previous incidents which would warrant such powers, especially the CSO, to be applied?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: On the whole, the threat of terrorism is real.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We have to be prepared for such an eventual attack.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It is important to note that this is not the first time the law enforcement agencies have been given special powers to deal with security issues.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The threat of terrorism comes in multiple and complex ways, which require swift and decisive action from our law enforcement and security agencies.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Therefore, it is necessary for our agencies to be equipped with the necessary powers to deal with the changing threats.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: As such, I support the Bill that is designed to protect our safety and security.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: First, to justify the broad measures, I am glad the Minister has given several examples on recent terrorist attacks, highlighting why the current laws are inadequate to deal with these and that is why a broad-based measure like this is necessary.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: My next point is that when the broad-based law is in place, sound and reasonable judgement by our law enforcement officers is needed.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And this judgement, within any enforcement agency, is enforced through the guidelines.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I recognise that it may not serve our interest to publish internal guidelines which could be potentially exploited by terrorists.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The need to articulate these broad principles was originally a concern for me, and I wanted to flag them out in my speech today.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad that the Minister has provided a clear explanation of these broad principles.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Next, I would like to touch on the issue of limiting communications in the event of a terrorist incident.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It makes sense not to have information posted online through public or open channels, be it social media or mainstream media.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: During a crisis, we all want to make sure that our immediate loved ones are safe and stay out of any possible danger zones.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
