text: So, a flurry of messages within closed networks can be expected.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Some would also argue that if this information does not spill over to the public networks, or to the social media, the risk of the terrorist getting wind of getting useful information is also quite limited.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, I hope the Government can invest in more efforts to share this aspect of the law with our people.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We must not stop anticipating in preparing to meet this threat.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In doing so, the challenges faced by other security forces and jurisdictions are informative.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Some members of the public have raised concerns about the provision to allow the Commissioner of Police to issue a CSO.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Their worry is that should this order be in effect, innocent bystanders who had unwittingly taken a photograph might be punished for a crime that they did not intend to commit.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In critical security situations, the safety of the public and officers is paramount.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have commanded a few operations during my 13 years with the Police Force.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This included gunman operations, kidnapping, manhunt for suspects who committed capital offences.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We realised that all operations are inherently risky, but those of this nature are especially dangerous to officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I had gone into dangerous situations with my officers, knowing full well that the risk can only be managed but not totally eliminated.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Tactical secrecy and integrity are critical to minimising risk.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I constantly worried about the loss of the element of surprise and our suspects ready to inflict grievous harm on my raiding officers.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I certainly could not allow prioritising any sharing of pictures involving the crime scene and the operations over the safety of officers and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Back then, I did not have to contend with Facebook "'live", "live" Twitter feeds and the fast spread of news through apps like WhatsApp.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I only had to manage and, very rarely, the odd photographer with telescopic lenses.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There were no drones to contend with; information sharing was rather limited and much slower through multimedia messaging service (MMS) and short message service (SMS).

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: During the trial of Ajmal Kasab, the prime accused of the Mumbai terrorist attack on 26 November 2008, Justices Aftab Alam and CK Prasad called the "live" coverage of the security operations "reckless".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: According to the newspaper, The Hindu, they said, "it is not possible to find out whether the security forces actually suffered any casualties or injuries on account of the way the operations were being displayed on the TV screen.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But it is beyond doubt that the way their operations were fully shown made the task of the security forces not only exceedingly difficult but also dangerous and risky." Our media personnel are responsible and will not seek to compromise operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So is the proposal to provide the Police with the power to take down autonomous vehicles in an attack, as these can compromise tactical secrecy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With regard to the issue of lack of transparency, every Police Officer seeks to live up to the Police's oath to protect life and property.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can trust that they will discharge their duties professionally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There is no reason to believe that we need allowing people on Facebook "live" or any other social media channels to monitor their operations in order that they may execute their mission professionally.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: While I support the proposals in this Bill, there must be greater public education on these matters.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: As we have done numerous simulated terrorist attacks to prepare our security agencies and other stakeholders, including the public, may I suggest that a mock CSO be included in future exercises as a way of promoting greater awareness on this matter?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, all over the world, terrorist attacks and serious incidents occur constantly.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Although there are no similar incidents happening in Singapore yet, we must always stay alert and be prepared for the contingencies.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We not only need to strengthen our security measures but also increase our enforcement powers in case a serious incident happens.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The CSO and the power given to the Police to restrict the use of drones are of great importance.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In order to successfully execute a high-risk operation, tactical secrecy is critical.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When I was a Police Officer, I took part in many enforcement operations.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Manhunt for suspects and raids are especially dangerous.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: When leading an operation, I was always concerned about external disturbances, for example, intrusion by innocent passers-by.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: If it was not handled properly, the lives of the Police Officers, victims and the public could be endangered.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With this new clause in place, the Police will be able to focus on the operations to arrest the terrorists and criminals.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The second important clause in this Bill is that the Police are given the power to ask operators to assist in the operation.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even though there have been no attacks in Singapore so far, there is no guarantee that such incidents will not happen here.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must be prepared and equipped, both at the national level where our security agencies have oversight and at the individual level.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We must cooperate and work together to protect our homeland.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In this respect, refraining from communicating at the sites of terror attacks is one of the ways individuals can cooperate with and assist our security forces.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Their actions, or rather, the lack of, could potentially save the lives of the unfortunate ones caught in the event and those of the men and women who risk their own to rescue them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, there are some concerns over the ban on the transmission of photos, videos, text and audio messages.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I think it is worth our time to examine more thoroughly the implications of this ban.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Today, rescuers have more than TV crews to worry about.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is what the Bill clearly seeks to prevent.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As part of our SGSecure campaign, our Home Team has been educating Singaporeans about what to do in the event of an attack – "Run, Hide, Tell".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We tell Singaporeans to move away from danger, stay out of sight, switch their phones to silent mode and provide information to the Police by calling, SMSing or using the SGSecure App.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, I hope the Ministry will consider allowing communications via other additional platforms in the event that these official channels become overloaded or malfunction.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: On the other hand, in case the terrorists or their sympathisers manage to transmit images or text in the midst of the mayhem, I hope we are equipped with the technology and know-how to jam the signals and prevent their broadcasts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Fines and jail-time are not going to be deterrents for them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Lastly, regarding the concerns by civil society groups over the definition of a "serious incident", I would like to caution that we should not assume that nothing would happen, even at seemingly small gatherings or peaceful protests.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is the duty of the Police to protect everyone, regardless of language, race, religion, political convictions and beliefs.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, to address the possibility of abuse whilst the communication ban is imposed, I would like to suggest we tap on the use of technology, such as equipping every policeman with a body video recorder.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The record could be reviewed by an independent committee and the composition of the members can be discussed to ensure independence.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Mandarin):   As the saying goes, "Don’t fear what is, fear what if".

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Every Singaporean must stay vigilant and must not think that terrorist attacks will never happen to them.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We do not have to be overly panicky, However, it is better to remain cautious.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They raised many useful points which I shall try to address.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Several Members asked about the definition of "serious incident", specifically the inclusion of "acts causing large-scale public disorder" and the illustration (d) in clause 3 which describes such an incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms K Thanaletchimi asked whether non-violent, passive protests are covered under the Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Kok Heng Leun, Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Louis Ng asked why the same powers to deal with terrorism are also available for large-scale public disorder.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Outside of the House, there were even assertions that POSSPA will be applied to "peaceful demonstrations".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The narrative goes something like this: first, the law allows POSSPA to be unlocked by the Minister for "peaceful protests".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Such protests can attract crowds of all sizes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There is no definition of what "large-scale public disorder" means, so the law could be applied to peaceful protests involving a small group of protestors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, the law potentially allows the oppression of protesters and will have a chilling effect on society.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The third limb, large-scale public disorder, is the subject of focus.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If a protest is really peaceful, there should be no concern whatsoever about falling within the third limb of "large-scale public disorder".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Illustration (d) in clause 3 makes it clear what we mean by "large-scale public disorder".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I should just quote to Members what it actually says.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It goes like this: "a sit-down demonstration for a cause attracts a large group of sympathisers who voluntarily join the sit-in.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For over a week, the group grows and the demonstrators start to occupy the publicly accessible paths and other open spaces in the central business district.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Their presence starts to impede the flow of vehicular and pedestrian traffic and interfere with normal trade or business activities in the area".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The demonstration "starts to impede the flow of…traffic and interfere with normal trade or business activities in the area".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The illustration shows quite clearly that not every protest will meet the high threshold to be considered a serious incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There must be significant disruption to ordinary Singaporeans trying to go about their daily business.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: People – motorists, commuters, passers-by, shopkeepers, workers – are agitated.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If it is not diffused, things could quickly turn chaotic.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some observers think such a situation is not intolerable, well within acceptable threshold.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun suggests that that situation should not be treated as a "serious incident".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, in such a situation, it is more likely that the Police will be asked: "Why are you allowing this chaos to unfold?", "Are you not worried something worse will happen?", "Can't you do something to prevent an escalation?" The Police will have to make a judgement call.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If they stick with existing policing powers, can they bring the situation under control?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What if the chaos spins out of control and there is loss of lives?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If they assess the need to seek powers under POSSPA, do they have enough justification?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What if they invoked POSSPA, and were, in fact, able to restore order but were then accused of having over-reacted?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That there was no need to have used POSSPA?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police will have to judge, the Minister will have to judge and decide.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This alone is not a low threshold to cross.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was after the Little India riot and, even then, it was tightly scoped to control the consumption of alcohol, to calm the situation and prevent further violence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police did not use any other power in POPA, even though they could.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Henry Kwek and Mr Kok Heng Leun asked why existing powers in other laws are not enough to deal with the large-scale public disorder scenarios described in illustrations (d) and (e).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Let us take illustration (d), although most of it applies to illustration (e) as well.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a large and protracted demonstration that is causing significant disruption to Singaporeans.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The demonstration keeps growing and things could get chaotic.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police may assess that they need to take measures to reduce the risk of property damage or prevent the crowd from further building up.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To do this, the Police may need to order nearby premises to close, impose a cordon, and direct people to stay out of the area.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The POSSPA powers are necessary to do this.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: No other laws have such provisions for such a situation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another example which occurred in Singapore: in the aftermath of the Little India riot, we activated POPA and used the POPA power to regulate conduct to stop the consumption of alcohol in public places in Little India.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Given the large crowds on weekends and public holidays, alcohol was assessed to be a significant risk factor for public disorder.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police did not have the power to do this outside of POPA until this Parliament passed new legislation under the Liquor Control Act to regulate the consumption of liquor in public places.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng, Ms Sylvia Lim and Ms K Thanaletchimi asked, how about the CSO?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Will it be used for the scenario set out in illustration (d)?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim said that law enforcement operations in large-scale public disorder would not tactically be sensitive to warrant CSO.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I have explained in my earlier speech that strict conditions must be met before the Commissioner of Police can issue a CSO.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It must be to protect the safety of the public or law enforcement operations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, it is not the case that when there is large-scale public disorder, all the special powers of POSSPA will be used to deal with the incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng asked if we could put a number to what is considered "large-scale".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: His question is understandable, but there is also no easy answer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The size of the protest is one of many factors.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It depends also where the protest is conducted, how it is conducted and its consequences on Singapore, whether intended by its organisers or not.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Mr Gan Thiam Poh has pointed out, a "peaceful demonstration" can quickly degenerate into violence and threaten public safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: An example is the London Riots in 2011.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It started off as a peaceful demonstration against a court ruling.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But degenerated into rioting, looting, setting buildings and vehicles on fire.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It spread to several cities over the course of the summer, including Birmingham, Leicester and Manchester.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In its trail, there were five dead and 205 injured, of which 189 were police officers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Property damage was estimated at £200 million, and the impact on the economy was significant.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Another example is the Charlottesville rally in 2017.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This took place against the backdrop of the controversial removal of Confederate monuments in parts of the United States (US), in response to the Charleston church shooting in 2015.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It started with a protest against the removal of a Confederate monument from a public park.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Protestors chanted racist slogans while carrying rifles and banners.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Virginia governor declared a state of emergency in order to have additional powers to safeguard public safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: One of the protestors rammed a car into a group of counter-protestors, killing one and injuring 19.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By the time the violence was over, there were three dead and at least 38 injured.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The point is this: peaceful intent does not guarantee peaceful outcomes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Having explained what "large scale public disorder" means, I will explain what it is not.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Where possible, we will, indeed, use existing laws to deal with such situations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, in Singapore, public assemblies are allowed in accordance with the law.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This comes under the framework of the POA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police regularly grant permits for public assemblies: last year alone, over 900.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have also set up the Speakers’ Corner for Singaporeans to organise events and demonstrations without having to apply for a permit, as long as certain conditions are met.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Many events take place at the Speakers’ Corner.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, the recent student demonstrations at Dublin Scioto High School in Columbus, Ohio.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: About 200 students sat outside the school in silence to protest gun violence in the wake of the Florida school shooting in February 2018.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There was no violence or large-scale public disorder in this example.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If such an event happens in Singapore, it can be dealt with using baseline policing powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, this is what we have done in the past.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: An example is the 2013 illegal protests at Merlion Park.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Around 100 foreigners gathered to protest the 2013 Malaysian elections on two different days.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We issued a total of 74 conditional warnings under the POA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, our record is clear and consistent – we have never used POPA against political dissent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is targeted at terrorist acts, serious violence affecting the public and large-scale public disorder.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Mr Christopher de Souza reminded us right at the beginning, "we do not want the Police to be unprepared, left inadequately protected because they are bereft of what they need to quell a threat".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In a serious incident, Singaporeans expect the Police to be able to act fast and to act decisively.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will next address Members' queries on the specific clauses.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked how the Police would deal with UAVs and AVs, if they are unable to find the operator.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clauses 28(2)(b)(ii) and 28(3)(b)(ii) empower Police Officers to act against UAVs and AVs directly, even if the operator cannot be located.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The priority is to stop the UAV or AV.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: AVs and UAVs are a relatively new area, which SAF and the Home Team are both working on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Home Team is also working on technology to target drones.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Christopher de Souza asked what would constitute "reasonable steps" under the law for companies or their officers to absolve themselves from liability for obligations under POSSPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will be a question of fact in each case whether a corporation's officer can be shown to have taken all reasonable steps to prevent or stop the commission of an offence by the corporation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To illustrate, clause 27 allows the Police to direct premises owners to take certain actions, like closing the premises.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng has asked why enhanced powers to stop and question individuals are needed under POSSPA, and whether these were excessive.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In a serious incident where POSSPA is activated, the Police need to be able to obtain information quickly in order to deal with the incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These enhanced powers make it clear that individuals have an onus to comply.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, when the Police are searching for an unknown terrorist suspect, to stop and question individuals to ask for information, they must be able to get the information quickly in order to trace the suspect.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Louis Ng asked for clarity on what constitutes "reasonable force".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In a serious incident, Police Officers and the public are faced with considerable danger, and the Police will need to be legally empowered to use lethal weapons, if indeed necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This means that the officer can use such force, as is reasonable in the circumstances, and no more.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police do not want to use lethal weapons unless all other options have been exhausted.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are clear internal Police procedures and rules to ensure that Police Officers act as such.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, Police Officers are typically equipped with a range of force options, including unarmed tactics, and non-lethal options, like batons and Tasers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Police Officers are trained to apply the appropriate force options in accordance with the situation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police have very rarely used lethal weapons.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, the Police came under criticism from some quarters, which suggested they should have used their firearms to deal with the rioters.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In that situation, the Police assessed the use of lethal weapons was not necessary and exercised restraint from using firearms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: On the other hand, there are times when the use of lethal weapons is necessary and justified.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Take the car that sped through concrete blocks at a Police checkpoint at the Shangri-la Dialogue in 2015.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was a high-profile event, with many foreign dignitaries in attendance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The risk that the car could be committing an act of terrorism was high.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: How would we know what was in the car?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng has also asked how SAF and the Police would coordinate operations on the ground.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police have worked closely with SAF to develop joint plans for terror attacks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Both forces have also exercised closely together on many counter-terrorism exercises.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In October 2016, the Police and SAF conducted a major joint Home Team-SAF counter-terrorism exercise.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was followed by Exercise Northstar in October 2017, a multi-agency counter-terrorism coordination exercise involving private stakeholders.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng, Mr Kok Heng Leun and Mr Louis Ng have also asked for clarifications on civilians assisting the Police under POSSPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, whether they will be sufficiently trained, and how we can ensure their safety.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I have mentioned in my earlier speech, civilian assistants can only exercise selected powers, under Police Officers' directions.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: There are no powers to compel civilians to aid the Police; they can only do so voluntarily.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Before requesting civilians to aid the Police, the Police will consider the suitability of the task at hand, and the risks to civilians.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As Mr Kok Heng Leun correctly points out, in some cases, it may be detrimental to deploy the civilians.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Mandarin saying is: 成 事 不 足, 败 事 有 余.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The volunteers will, therefore, not be assigned to tasks that will put them in harm’s way or which they are quite incapable of performing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police conducted an exercise in October 2016.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The scenario involved multiple gunmen attacks at a shopping mall.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In this exercise, mall security officers assisted the Police by evacuating the public to safety, and no more than that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is an example of the kind of roles civilian assistants may be tasked with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng has also asked about the class of public officers who may be prescribed as "law enforcement officers".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As the threats continue to evolve over time, our operational needs will change.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This provision simply allows the Minister to prescribe specific groups of public officers with specialised skills to assist the Police in responding to the serious incidents, for example, cybersecurity specialists or whoever else.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would, first, like to acknowledge the support that Mr Melvin Yong and Mr Desmond Choo have voiced for the Bill, in particular for the CSO.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As former Police Officers, they understand the challenges and risks that Police Officers face, and the need for the special powers in this Bill to deal with serious incidents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked whether the CSO will only be activated for exceptional situations where operational secrecy and integrity are critical for saving lives and protecting property.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng suggested adopting a Code of Conduct for journalists and using the CSO as a last resort.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Henry Kwek asked whether the public will be notified when the CSO is place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The short answer to Mr Desmond Choo's question is yes, as I have explained earlier in my speech.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng's suggestion on the media Code of Conduct is a useful one which we will consider.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But the fact is this: in a serious incident, we cannot rely solely on a Code of Conduct.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police will publicise the CSO through all its public communications platforms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Other Members raised some concerns on the CSO which can be grouped into four categories: one, whether the CSO will stop people from sending information to the Police, or sending updates on their situation to their loved ones; two, whether the CSO would lead to less accountability for the actions of the Police; three, why should mere making of films be banned; and four, how the CSO will be enforced in practice.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, when the Police look into reports lodged on breaches of the CSO, it will consider the circumstances of the sender and if the breach could reasonably have been avoided or should have been avoided, if the actions posed safety risk to the public or to the law enforcement officers, or if the leaked film exposed sensitive tactical information of the law enforcement activity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Some Members, like Mr Melvin Yong, Ms Thanaletchimi, and Mr Gan Thiam Poh, asked whether the CSO would stop people from communicating information to the Police or discourage them from doing so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police are more aware than anyone else of this.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The objective of the CSO is to protect the integrity of specific security operations at a particular location and for a limited time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Outside of the scope of the CSO, there is no restriction on communications in general.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The public will be encouraged to submit information to the Police via the "999" hotline or through the iWitness and SGSecure platforms.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I hope this assurance addresses Ms Sylvia Lim's concerns.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim said that without film or photo, the burden would fall on the complainant to prove the complaint.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: She also cited the example of Mr Tomlinson at the G20 Summit in 2009.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In the first instance, it is unlikely that the CSO would have been issued in a public order incident like the one she described.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It was not the kind of scenario in which we had envisioned CSO to be issued.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But with or without footage, any person with a complaint of misconduct by Police Officers can lodge a Police report, and they regularly do.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Without footage, Ms Sylvia Lim is right that it may be harder for the Police to verify the complaint.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, the Police's investigations do not start and end with photo or video evidence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They can interview the parties involved and gather other evidence to establish the validity of the claim.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police have always taken a serious view of all complaints made against our officers and will thoroughly investigate these complaints.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the complaint is substantiated, the Police will not hesitate to take action against any errant officer.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun also asked whether the Police will use the powers under the CSO to delete videos and photos of abuse of powers by the Police.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is a criminal offence to dispose of evidence and Police officers cannot do that.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh suggested equipping every Police Officer with a body-worn camera to mitigate the risk of unfair allegations when a CSO is in place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a helpful suggestion, and we will look into it.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, the Police have equipped a number of their frontline officers with body-worn cameras to facilitate investigations and the gathering of evidence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The footage from these cameras is also helpful for any allegations of wrongdoing.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is on top of the in-vehicle cameras that Police have.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These cameras will continue to operate when a CSO is in place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This leaves me with the third and fourth group of issues under the CSO, which I will address together.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Besides issues of accountability, Ms Sylvia Lim expressed discomfort with extending the CSO to the making of relevant pictures and films.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim's view is that mere making of the film does not cause harm and should be allowed.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Louis Ng also asked how the CSO will be enforced by officers on the ground.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, there could be many people using their phones at the same time for different reasons.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As I explained earlier, during a serious incident, the Police will not have the bandwidth to investigate every person who is recording a film or picture to ascertain its true intent.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also acknowledged from her experience as a former Police Officer that this is a challenge.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police will exercise discretion and take into consideration the circumstances which the recorder was in and if the breach could not have been reasonably avoided.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This Bill puts the onus on the individuals to not arouse suspicion of malicious intent not because the Police want to make things difficult, but because of exigency.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: By doing so, the Police have a straightforward enforcement aim to make sure no one is recording.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If it were not spelt out this clearly, then you could have a situation of confusion: what exactly are the Police trying to enforce against?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun asked a similar point: why is the possession of materials likely to prejudice public order a criminal offence?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is why MHA earlier spoke to the local media to hear their concerns and discuss how we can work closely to ensure that the CSO does not disrupt their ability to report the news for documentation purposes.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The local media also raised concerns similar to Members and the general public.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, how to ensure that those caught in the incident can report to the Police?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We have taken this into account and, in my earlier speech, I also talked about the importance of post-incident reporting and how we will allow the media to record incidents for subsequent reporting.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun asked if there was a public consultation for this Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We studied international incidents, spoke to our law enforcement counterparts and gleaned learning points on how to deal with these incidents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Then we consulted key stakeholders who would be directly affected by the exercise of specific powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This was the same approach for the POA amendment Bill, as well as the Infrastructure Protection Bill just last year.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I will now move on to the issue of safeguards for POSSPA powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Henry Kwek has asked whether there will be any limits to the duration the provisions will stay in effect.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We do not intend to use the POSSPA powers for longer than is absolutely necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After a serious incident has been resolved, one of our key priorities is to work with the affected communities to return to normalcy as soon as possible.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Having an Activation Order longer than necessary does not help.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun asked why the failure to publish would not invalidate an order.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: All that clause 8(3) does is to ensure that the mere failure to publish the Activation Order does not invalidate the need for the Commissioner of Police to issue a special authorisation and deploy the Police Officers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This does not diminish accountability of the Minister.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It can happen that the Commissioner of Police may need to act quickly and issue the special authorisations.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He should not be prevented from doing so just because of a delay in publishing the Minister's Activation Order, which is a technicality.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is what the provision seeks to protect, nothing more.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Melvin Yong asked whether a new Activation Order would be needed if subsequent incidents are unrelated to the first incident for which the Activation Order was made.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: For example, if a large-scale public disorder occurs that is unrelated to a terrorist act for which an Activation Order has been issued, the Minister would need to issue a new Activation Order to be able to exercise POSSPA powers for the new incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, Mr Melvin Yong makes a more important point about whose judgement it will be in deciding whether the two incident areas are related.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It will have to be a professional assessment made by the Police based on the information at hand.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Commissioner will have to decide before he issues a special authorisation.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Kok Heng Leun raised a similar line of query in many parts of his speech.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I listened carefully and I must say, for me, it contrasted very much with Ms Sylvia Lim's speech, which I believe to be well-informed by her professional experience as a Police Officer and her legal training.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I reflected on Mr Kok Heng Leun's point, and I think his main discomfort has to do with the discretion given to the Minister and the Commissioner of Police; whether we should trust them to act honourably at all times or whether we should curtail their discretion and not leave it to chance.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Therefore, he asked whether we can impose conditions under which the powers are used and whether these conditions can be written into the Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In my view, it is not unreasonable to consider such risks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: In fact, Mr Kok Heng Leun cited the ISA in which we subject the decisions of the Minister to the concurrence by the President on the advice of a Special Advisory Committee.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This shows clearly that the Government − this Government − is not averse to introducing such checks if there are good justifications to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And on a day-to-day basis, Ministers and the Commissioner of Police do not have as much latitude in their exercise of powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, the POSSPA Bill is designed for serious incidents as per clause 3 where we envision the Police to be in a race against time.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Hypothetically, suppose terrorists have taken some Singaporeans hostage, can we afford to put the rescue operations on hold while Parliament debates whether the Minister's Activation Order or the Commissioner's CSO are justified?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And in a terror situation, things can change by the minute.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Supposing in the meantime, the terrorists start to harm the hostages and we decide we can no longer wait.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Police mount a rescue operation but, predictably, there was live coverage of the Police operations online.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Would it not weigh on our conscience that we have not given the hostages or the security personnel the best chance of survival because the CSO was not authorised in time?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ultimately, it boils down to this: there is a risk of too much discretion, but there is also a risk of too much delay.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Members will have to weigh which is the bigger risk in a serious incident, which has the graver consequence.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This tension was also highlighted by Mr Christopher de Souza, who concluded that "this Bill equips the Police with the level of power necessary to quell danger and neutralise an escalating target".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Once the threshold of a serious incident is crossed, we must give the Police sufficient latitude to act decisively and respond to whatever the threat may be.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And I think that sums it up aptly.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: You need the muscle; you need the flexibility in a serious incident.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: After the incident has been dealt with, and the danger has passed, we can have a debate, including here in Parliament, about whether the Minister and the Police did the right thing, and hold them to account.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We did that for the Little India riot.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The inquiry was fairly extended, and the inquiry certainly did point out areas that the members of the panel thought the Government had fallen short on.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: But you do that after the incident has been dealt with.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We, therefore, agree that it is important for the public to be aware of the obligations under the new Bill when an Activation Order is in place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Ms Thanaletchimi, Mr Ang Wei Neng and Mr Desmond Choo have all asked how we intend to do so.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: MHA will also continue to inform the public on the key points of POSSPA, like what to do when a CSO is in place.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We will do so via our Home Team outreach channels, such as SGSecure.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To increase awareness, Mr Desmond Choo and Mr Ang Wei Neng have suggested conducting exercises for the public on how the powers will be used, especially for the CSO.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This is a very helpful suggestion and is something that the Police will consider.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The special powers under POSSPA are needed to deal with serious incidents, like terrorist attacks.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The special powers, which come with safeguards, will be used judiciously.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: As the threats have changed and technologies have changed, we must ensure that the Police are empowered to respond to these new threats.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I was listening very intently to her argument.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: There are two points which I still feel a bit uncomfortable.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: One is the definition of the "illustration" in question, which was illustration (d).

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Just by the mere words of it, to be honest, I do not sense that kind of seriousness as the Second Minister has described and her subsequent elaboration of what the situation could be.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: So, I would like to ask maybe, in this Bill itself, there should be some change of wording in that part of the illustration whereby it is not just about a disruption to daily businesses, but a protracted disruption.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: That would make it sound in terms of the severity, in comparison to what the Second Minister has said.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: At the same time, when things are still quite peaceful at that moment, any kind of Police intervention may, under this Bill, actually cause even more problems subsequently.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: The second one is about asking for accountability from the Minister and the Commissioner.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I think just because this Bill is so severe in terms of the action that comes with it, I am asking if that is really not because there is a mistrust, I guess a kind of accountability.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: That is why, in my speech, I did say that as much as time can permit without affecting the expediency of the Police action, I think even an official report on the decision of the Minister or the Commissioner would be very important to be submitted to Parliament in that process.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: I think that is what we really need in terms of accountability.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: That is to the first question that the Member asked.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: To the second question on accountability, Mr Kok Heng Leun is looking at it from the point of view of whether or not you trust the individuals.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I would put to Mr Kok to look at it from the point of view of the person who has to exercise these powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: What is the weight of the office that he will feel?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: His immediate thought is, “This is serious stuff.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I can be asked a question in Parliament and probably not just one.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Can I justify this action?” Is this not accountability?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Does this not already encapsulate what Mr Kok says?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If it were such a low threshold, if it was so easy for the Minister to be able to activate POSSPA, or the powers, then I do not think, in 60 years, the number of times in which you can attribute POSSPA powers to have been invoked, to be countable on one hand.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: With regard to the second reply, I think we are sort of in the same place and, in a way, I do agree that it is a heavy and difficult decision.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: That is why I think that the more difficult and heavier it is, the procedure of accountability becomes even more important.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: That is why I am not suggesting that we have to call Parliament up to have a deliberation on that immediately.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: But, in certain circumstances, if Parliament needs to sit to deliberate on something really important, I think Parliament has that moral responsibility to do that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: In this particular case, I am talking about a report after the activation would really be very important to actually lay out how the decision was being made, the threshold we need, without asking for Committees of Inquiry (COIs) and things like that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: So, it is just about a certain procedure so that we could also respect the kind of heavy responsibility that these people are making, and they are affecting every individual, at least within that vicinity, of course, also the whole of Singapore.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: He does not need a procedure for that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: Of course, we can always file a PQ in Parliament, but I am just seeking a kind of procedure rather than each time relying on the PQs.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: And we only meet once a month for that.

speaker: Mr Kok Heng Leun
text: So, in that moment, as soon as it can, if possible, I do not find that it is a problem to submit a report.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Does he not think that the public would already expect a report to be tabled?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And that even without a PQ, any self-respecting Minister knows that he has to respond.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I do not think you need to write it into a Bill.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The Minister will have to stand for election.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: We do not know what timeframe, but he will have to, at some point.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And if he has not thought about accountability, something must be seriously wrong.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: So, I am quite baffled by Mr Kok's insistence on this point.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is a concern that I am not quite sure I understand fully because there is already nothing that prevents Parliament from debating incidents.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Far smaller-scale incidents have been discussed at length in Parliament.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: And when a serious incident happens, I cannot imagine that it will not be brought to Parliament for discussion.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Today, SAF servicemen may already be deployed under section 201C of the SAF Act to assist civilian authorities like the Police.

text: The amendments made clear such activities can be considered law enforcement activities under POSSPA.

text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move amendments* 5 to 7, standing in the Minister's name, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Amendments 5 to 7 change the definition of "serviceman" to refer to a serviceman who is deployed for duty under section 201C of the SAF Act by MINDEF and is authorised under section 201E of the SAF Act to exercise powers provided for under section 201C(9) of the same Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: It is through section 201E of the SAF Act that the Minister for Defence exercises control over which powers SAF servicemen are authorised to exercise when assisting civilian authorities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, may I seek your permission to move the two amendments together as they are related?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move amendments* 1 and 2 standing in the Minister's name, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Instead, when an activation order by the Minister for Home Affairs is in place, the Commissioner of Police will make a request for SAF servicemen to support the Police with selected POSSPA powers as are necessary.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Under these circumstances, MINDEF will authorise the powers that SAF servicemen may exercise under the SAF Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I explained during the Second Reading this is to ensure a clearly defined command and control over all deployments of SAF servicemen in support of civilian authorities, including for serious incidents under POSSPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move amendments* 1 and 2 standing in the Minister's name, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These amendments are needed for the similar reason as for clause 11.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: SAF servicemen will no longer be given a special authorisation by the Commissioner of Police under POSSPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move the amendment* standing in the Minister's name, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clause 13 is amended for the same reason given for changes to clauses 11 and 12.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Our intent for powers exercisable by SAF servicemen to be authorised under the SAF Act and not by the Commissioner of Police under POSSPA.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move amendments* 1 to 4 standing in the Minister's name, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Clause 15 currently describes what POSSPA powers SAF servicemen can exercise and how they can exercise them.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amendments delete SAF servicemen from this clause.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move the amendment* standing in the Minister's name, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amendment will ensure that the Minister for Home Affairs can also give directions to discontinue telecommunications services so as to avoid endangering the safety of SAF servicemen during an ongoing law enforcement activity.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, may I seek your permission to move the three amendments together as they are related?

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to move amendments* 1 to 3 standing in the Minister's name, as indicated in the Order Paper Supplement.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amendments to clause 50 are to make it clear that POSSPA does not affect an SAF serviceman's powers under Part VII and VIIA of the SAF Act which relate to emergency powers of SAF servicemen and the powers SAF servicemen can exercise in aid of civilian authorities.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The exercise of powers under the SAF Act will be subject to the safeguards that exist within the SAF Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: Mr Chairman, I beg to introduce a new clause entitled "Amendment of the Singapore Armed Forces Act".

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: These are no more than what is in clause 15(6) of the Bill if we did not amend that earlier.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: If the Commissioner of Police does not request for the military's assistance on certain duties, the SAF servicemen will not be able to exercise those powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I next refer Members to the new clause 60(a) to (d) and (f).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amendments to section 201C(9)(b), (c), (d) and (e) have the effect of suspending these powers whenever similar powers under section 201C(9)(f) are exercised by the SAF servicemen activated to support the civilian authority using POSSPA powers.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The amendments made clear that the overlapping SAF Act powers are suspended when SAF servicemen are authorised with similar POSSPA powers under section 201C(9)(f).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: The definition of similar powers is described in new clause 60(f) which inserts a new subsection (11) in section 201C of the SAF Act.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: However, the powers in 201C(9)(b), (c), (d) and (e) remain available to servicemen outside of a target area even during an activation period.

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: I refer Members to new clause 60(g) and (h).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: They amend section 201F of the SAF Act to level the thresholds for use of legal weapons with that in POSSPA, only for the POSSPA powers that are exercisable by SAF servicemen under section 201C(9)(f).

speaker: Mrs Josephine Teo
text: This will ensure that penalties for public safety and security offences are aligned across the two legislation.
